edges.description: The deformation an impact imposes on neurons is itself enough to start tau pathology.
Impacts injure the small vessels around which the CTE lesion forms; vascular injury markers rise with years of exposure.
edges.target: Microvascular Injury and Blood-Brain Barrier Leakage

edges.description: Repetitive head impacts trigger accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau at the depths of cortical sulci around small vessels. A finite-element head model offers a biomechanical reason for that location: the strain an impact produces in brain tissue is greatest at the depths of sulci. The model links where tissue is loaded to where pathology is found; it does not show how strain leads to tau accumulation. The model is curated as a computational model in Traumatic_Brain_Injury.
Hyperphosphorylated, mislocalized tau in strained neurons is the cellular start of the tangles that accumulate at the sulcal depths.
Vascular injury is accompanied by microglial recruitment.
edges.source: Microvascular Injury and Blood-Brain Barrier Leakage

edges.description: Activated microglia carry part of the effect of head impacts on tau accumulation.
Tau pathology in CTE is accompanied by supportive TDP-43 neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions in limbic regions.
Combined tau and TDP-43 pathology drives progressive neuronal loss and the clinical syndrome, including motor neuron disease in a subset.
edges.target: Neurodegeneration with Cognitive, Behavioral, and Motor Decline

nodes.description: Years of head-impact exposure, and the development and severity of CTE, are associated with reactive microglial morphology and more CD68-positive (activated, phagocytic) microglia in the dorsolateral frontal cortex. In a path model of 66 football players and 16 controls, exposure raises CD68 microglial density independently of age, and part of exposure's effect on tau pathology runs through that rise, placing chronic microglial activation on the path from impacts to the tauopathy.

evidence.reference_title: Microglial neuroinflammation contributes to tau accumulation in chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
evidence.snippet: Duration of RHI exposure and the development and severity of CTE were associated with reactive microglial morphology and increased numbers of CD68 immunoreactive microglia in the DLF.

nodes.description: Head impacts injure the cortical microvasculature. In post-mortem dorsolateral frontal cortex the vascular injury markers ICAM1, VCAM1 and CRP are raised in CTE above both exposed and unexposed controls, ICAM1 staining is concentrated on vessels and astrocytes at the sulcal depths in high-stage disease, and perivascular serum albumin, a sign of blood-brain barrier leakage, is present in every exposed individual. The findings are associations in human tissue; the order of vascular injury and tau accumulation is not established by them.

evidence.reference_title: Vascular injury is associated with repetitive head impacts and tau pathology in chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
evidence.snippet: Levels of vascular injury-associated markers ICAM1, VCAM1, and CRP were increased in CTE compared to RHI-exposed and -naïve controls.

evidence.reference_title: Vascular injury is associated with repetitive head impacts and tau pathology in chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
evidence.snippet: Multifocal perivascular immunoreactivity for serum albumin was present in all RHI-exposed individuals.

nodes.description: Progressive neurodegeneration produces the CTE clinical syndrome: impaired memory and executive function, behavioral and mood disturbances, parkinsonism, and, in a subset of cases, motor neuron disease. The motor-neuron-disease subset links CTE to the elevated ALS risk reported in professional contact-sport athletes.

evidence.snippet: parkinsonism, and, occasionally, motor neuron disease are seen in affected individuals.

nodes.description: The pathognomonic lesion of CTE is the accumulation of abnormal hyperphosphorylated tau (p-tau) in neurons and astroglia clustered around small blood vessels at the depths of cortical sulci in an irregular pattern. This perivascular, sulcal-depth distribution distinguishes CTE from other tauopathies such as Alzheimer disease and progressive supranuclear palsy. Pathology progresses in an ordered way, from focal perivascular epicentres in the frontal neocortex to widespread tauopathy including the medial temporal lobe, the basis of the four-stage (I-IV) severity scale.

nodes.description: The initiating exposure is repeated concussive and subconcussive head impacts sustained over years, as in contact sports, military blast injury, and other causes of recurrent head trauma. This mechanical exposure triggers the downstream neurodegenerative tauopathy after a long latency.

evidence.reference_title: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy: a potential late effect of sport-related concussive and subconcussive head trauma.
evidence.snippet: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a form of neurodegeneration believed to result from repeated head injuries.

nodes.description: High-strain-rate deformation of neurons, with no other insult, drives tau hyperphosphorylation and its mislocalization from axons to dendritic spines, with synaptic deficits that depend on tau. The effect runs through the tau kinases GSK3B and CDK5: inhibiting them, or deleting tau, reverses it. The regions that bear the most strain in a computational model of injury are the early sites of tangles in CTE brains. This is cell-culture evidence for a direct path from impact mechanics to tau pathology, not a demonstration in human tissue.

evidence.reference_title: Mechanical injuries of neurons induce tau mislocalization to dendritic spines and tau-dependent synaptic dysfunction.
evidence.snippet: The mechanical energy associated with high-strain rate deformation alone can induce tau mislocalization to dendritic spines and synaptic deficits in cultured rat hippocampal neurons.

evidence.reference_title: Mechanical injuries of neurons induce tau mislocalization to dendritic spines and tau-dependent synaptic dysfunction.
evidence.snippet: These cellular changes are mediated by tau hyperphosphorylation and can be reversed through inhibition of GSK3β and CDK5 or genetic deletion of tau.

nodes.description: Beyond the dominant tauopathy, CTE shows supportive TDP-43 proteinopathy: TDP-43-immunoreactive neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions in the hippocampus, anteromedial temporal cortex, and amygdala. This places CTE within the family of TDP-43 proteinopathies and is mechanistically relevant to the motor neuron disease seen in a subset of cases.
